title: Gandhi's Sandals for General Smuts
text:
For years in South Africa, Mohandas Gandhi led the Indian community's campaigns of civil disobedience against discriminatory laws. His chief opponent in government was General Jan Smuts, who more than once had him jailed. Gandhi never treated Smuts as an enemy. He negotiated with him patiently, kept his word, and in January 1914 suspended a planned march rather than take advantage of a railway strike that was troubling the government.

The two men finally reached an agreement in 1914, and Gandhi prepared to leave for India. Before he sailed, he sent Smuts a gift: a pair of leather sandals he had made himself while in prison.

Smuts kept them. In 1939, for Gandhi's seventieth birthday, he wrote an essay for a commemorative volume. He said he had worn the sandals for many summers, "even though I may feel that I am not worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man." He also wrote that it had been his fate to be the antagonist of a man for whom, even then, he had the highest respect.
lesson: You can oppose someone firmly and still treat them with courtesy and good faith. Respect shown to an opponent is often returned, sometimes decades later.
source: Jan Christiaan Smuts, "Gandhi's Political Method," in Mahatma Gandhi: Essays and Reflections on His Life and Work, ed. S. Radhakrishnan (1939)
